extracted.subtask_description: A research proof in analytic number theory establishing the existence of bounded gaps between primes by constructing weight functions, estimating bilinear sums, and combining strengthened distribution results for primes in arithmetic progressions. The paper develops Type I/II/III estimates, factorization of moduli, and uses deep exponential-sum bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the main inequality to prove (target)
rubrics_metrics.description: S2 - (log^3 x) S1 > 0 (equation (2.3)): With an appropriate choice of A(n) one must prove S2 - (log^3 x) S1 > 0 so that for sufficiently large x there is an n ~ x such that the k0-tuple contains at least two primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central quantitative target whose positive sign yields the existence of bounded prime gaps. All parameter choices and estimates are arranged to make the main term dominate the error to obtain this inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible k-tuple (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: We say that H is admissible if V_p #{h_i (mod p)} < p for every prime p (definition following (1.3)). Theorem 1 assumes T_L is admissible with k0 > 3.5 x 10^6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissibility is required so that there is no local obstruction modulo any prime to having all shifts n + h_i possibly simultaneously prime; admissibility of the chosen fixed tuple underlies the sieve construction and main-term evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical hypothesis on tuple size for unconditional bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1: Suppose that TL is admissible with k0 > 3.5 x 10^6. Then there are infinitely many n such that the k0-tuple contains at least two primes; consequently liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) < 7 x 10^7 (equations (1.4)-(1.5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit (crude) numerical thresholds (k0 > 3.5e6 and the resulting bound 7e7) are part of the proved result; the paper notes these are not optimal and could be improved with sharper evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of weight function A(n) with modulus constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A(n) is taken of the form A(n) = sum_{d | P(n), d \ V} mu(d) g(d) (equation (2.11)), where g is supported on d < D and the sum runs over d dividing P(n) but constrained by d \ V (i.e., d free of large prime divisors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing the constraint d \ V (moduli free from large prime divisors) is central: it leaves the main term essentially unchanged while allowing stronger control of the error via factorization of d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of D (cutoff for divisor sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set D = x^{1/4 + w} with small positive w (equation (2.5)). The paper contrasts D = x^{1/4 + w} (needed for main-term size) with D = x^{1/4 - eps} (where Bombieri–Vinogradov suffices for error control but main-term relation (2.6) cannot be made valid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing D = x^{1/4 + w} gives the desired main-term magnitude while necessitating the additional constraint d \ V and the new factorization technique to bound errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint that moduli be free of large prime divisors (d \ V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: contributions from terms with d having a large prime divisor are relatively small; hence impose constraint d \ V in the definition of A(n) so that the resulting main term remains large while errors become tractable (discussion following (2.6)-(2.8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction is used to enable factoring d as d = r q with controllable r and q ranges, which is key to applying factorization/well-factorability ideas (Iwaniec) and to bounding sums involving A(·; d, c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization lemma for d (existence of r, q with r in a chosen range)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 4: Suppose d > D1, d \ V and (d, V0) < D1. For any R* satisfying D1 < R* < d, there is a factorization d = r q such that D1 R* < r < R* and (q, Vq) = 1 (equation (3.7) and statement of Lemma 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This flexible factorization (d = r q with r in a chosen dyadic window) underlies the 'well-factorable' treatment of the characteristic function of allowed d and is crucial for Type I/II/III estimates and bounding errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 2: L^1-type bound on sums of A(r; d, c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 2 (equation (2.12)): For 1 < i < k0 we have sum_{d < D^2, d \ V} sum_{c in C_i(d)} |A(r; d, c)| << x^{1 - A} (with implied saving), i.e., a strong mean bound for |A(·; d, c)| over allowed d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mean bound (combined with Cauchy) is the key technical estimate required to control the error terms; the rest of the paper is devoted to proving it by reducing to Type I/II/III estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I / Type II / Type III convolution classification and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper classifies arising Dirichlet convolutions into three types with specific support conditions (see (2.13) and conditions (Ai)-(A5)). Type I: xi < N < X2; Type II: X2 < N < 2x^{1/2}; Type III: convolutions of shape alpha * beta1 * beta2 with (A4)-(A5) constraints including N3 < N2 < N1, M N1 < x^{1+o(1)}, and size/range relations (A4)-(A5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must check which type a given convolution belongs to; different analytic techniques (dispersion method + factorization, Birch–Bombieri/Deligne estimates, incomplete Kloosterman bounds) handle each type. The hypotheses Ai–A5 (support, divisor bounds, Siegel–Walfisz-type uniformity) must be verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siegel–Walfisz uniformity assumption for coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For any q, r and a with (a, r) = 1, the 'Siegel–Walfisz' assumption is required: sum_{n = a (mod r), (n, q r) = 1} beta(n) << N tau(q)^{O(1)} with certain uniformity and exponential decay (stated after (A3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uniform distribution in residue classes for the multiplicative coefficients beta is assumed for the convolutions; it allows use of the dispersion method and large-modulus estimates in the Type I/II treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bombieri–Vinogradov and when it suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem (level of distribution 1/2) suffices to bound the error when D = x^{1/4 - eps}, but not when D = x^{1/4 + w}; hence the paper develops a strengthened approach applicable when moduli are free of large prime divisors (discussion around (2.5)-(2.7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper exploits that the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem gives acceptable error for smaller D, but to get the necessary main-term size one must enlarge D and use the d \ V restriction plus factorization to recover control of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the dispersion method and reduction to incomplete Kloosterman sums
rubrics_metrics.description: In Type I and II estimates the dispersion method (Fouvry–Iwaniec; Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec) is combined with the factorization (2.8) to reduce the problem to estimating certain incomplete Kloosterman sums, where saving a small power of x (via Weil-type bounds) suffices (discussion in §2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates the analytic route: factor moduli, apply dispersion to convert sums into exponential sums/Kloosterman-type objects, then apply Weil bounds (or variants) to extract the needed saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type III reliance on deep algebraic-geometry estimates (Birch–Bombieri/Deligne)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Type III estimate essentially relies on the Birch–Bombieri result (appendix to [6]) which in turn relies on Deligne's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis for varieties over finite fields (Weil Conjectures) (discussion in §2). Lemma 12 gives bounds T(k,...) << (k, q)^{1/2} q^{3/2+eps}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certain three-factor convolutions one must invoke deep results (Deligne-style exponential-sum bounds) to get the required exponents; the paper states explicitly where such algebraic-geometry input is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial decomposition / Heath-Brown identity usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 6 gives a combinatorial decomposition (special case of Heath–Brown identity) expressing A(n) as convolutions of short supported sequences so that the problem reduces to estimating convolutions of controlled lengths (see §6 and Lemma 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial splitting is the standard step to reduce sums over primes/weights to a bounded number of convolution types (Type I/II/III) amenable to analytic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieving / main-term evaluation conventions and parameter conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions: all quantities depending only on the fixed tuple T_L are regarded as constants; e denotes any sufficiently small positive constant; A,B,C denote sufficiently large/small constants whose meanings may vary; constants implied in big-O depend at most on e and A (notation in §2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bookkeeping/notation conventions guide which dependencies are allowed in estimates and which quantities are treated as absolute versus parameter-dependent. They are required to interpret asymptotic statements and to choose parameter hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper/lower bound strategy for S1 and S2 (main-term vs error control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish an upper bound for S1 (Section 4) of the form Si <= (main constant) x (log D)^{k0+2l0} + o(x(log D)^{k0+2l0}), and a lower bound for S2 (Section 5) S2 = k0 T2 x + O(x^{1-A}); combine these (with Theorem 2 controlling errors) to obtain S2 - (log^3 x) S1 > 0 (see (4.20), (5.6), (5.7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof strategy is to explicitly compute main terms and show the positive difference after absorbing all error bounds; the bounds involve combinatorial/arithmetic constants computed via multiplicative functions and require precise control of secondary terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Möbius inversion and Ramanujan sums in residue-class counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical steps repeatedly use Möbius inversion to handle coprimality constraints and Ramanujan sums (C_q(a)) for handling additive characters over reduced residue classes (see notation and manipulations in §2 and proofs of Lemmas 1–3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard analytic number theory tools used throughout to convert congruence / coprimality constraints into multiplicative/arithmetic functions amenable to Dirichlet series / contour integration techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter hierarchy and small/large parameter choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Several small/large parameters are introduced with hierarchical relationships (e.g., 0 < w small, l0 = 180, D0 = exp{C l0 k0}, V = product_{p < D1} p, D1, V0, choices for xi, x2 in (2.13)), and constraints like x^{1/4} < d < D^2, D2 = x^{1/2 - eps}, etc., are enforced to place sums in the right ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper selection and ordering of these parameters (and verifying the inequalities among them) is part of the 'rubric' for constructing the proof: each analytic bound assumes those relations, and the validity of Type I/II/III categorizations depends on them.
